text: It's 7:42 AM. You're the overnight SOC analyst at a mid-sized company, and your SIEM fires an alert: a workstation on the internal network is making repeated outbound connections to an unfamiliar external address on port 4444, roughly once every sixty seconds. Nothing about this alert explains itself — it's up to you to work it, and every chapter of this course just became the tool you work it with.

Networking fundamentals first: the source is internal, the destination is unrecognized, port 4444 isn't a common well-known port, and a quick look in Wireshark shows a clean handshake followed by that same steady beaconing pattern from the kill-chain lesson. Then core security concepts — the CIA triad frames confidentiality as the immediate concern, risk looks high on both likelihood and impact, and you check the account's authorization model to see exactly what it can actually reach.

That beaconing pattern to an external address matches malware and command-and-control behavior from Chapter 6, not a web application attack or a straightforward network attack — which tells you this almost certainly started earlier, upstream of this alert. So you isolate the workstation, exactly what the incident-response policy from Chapter 7 calls for, and you document every step, because compliance frameworks like NIST and ISO 27001 require that record regardless of how this turns out.

Zoom out and that's the whole course: Chapters 1 through 3 gave you the networking fundamentals, 4 and 5 gave you the core security concepts, Chapter 6 taught attack recognition, Chapter 7 taught policy and defense, and this chapter put a lab, Wireshark, and a full kill-chain case study underneath all of it.

That's the course, complete — from 'what is a network' to working a live-looking incident with the right concept from the right chapter, on demand. Next up in this path: Windows, Linux and Security Administration, where you start defending the actual operating systems underneath everything you just learned.
